etymology: Hebrew beyth lebaoth, “house of lionesses,” a town of the southern allotment given over to the tribe of Simeon within the inheritance of Judah.
biblical_def: Beth-lebaoth was a town of the dry south country named among the cities given to the tribe of Simeon, whose portion was carved out of the wide inheritance of Judah. When Joshua and Eleazar the priest cast the lot at Shiloh, the children of Simeon received their cities within the borders of the children of Judah, “for the part of the children of Judah was too much for them” (Jos 19:9), and among these is reckoned Beth-lebaoth, the house of lionesses (Jos 19:6). The name remembers a land where the lion couched in the thickets of the Negeb, a place few would have called desirable, and yet the LORD numbered it among the goodly heritage He measured to His people. The dictionary does not labour the obscure points of its situation; it honours that the bounds of Simeon were not the work of chance. He who divided to the nations their inheritance and set the bounds of the people apportioned even this little southern town, that no part of His people’s heritage should fall outside His care (Deu 32:8; Act 17:26). The lines were fallen unto Simeon in pleasant places, and Beth-lebaoth stands a witness that the least-known portion is yet a goodly heritage when it is the gift of God.

etymology: Hebrew beyth markaboth, “house of chariots,” a town of the south country reckoned to the tribe of Simeon within the inheritance of Judah.
biblical_def: Beth-marcaboth, the house of chariots, was a town of the Negeb numbered among the cities given to the tribe of Simeon, whose portion lay within the over-large inheritance of Judah (Jos 19:5). The name suggests a place once set for chariots, perhaps a station of war or commerce in the open south, yet in the apportioning of the land it is simply one of the cities the LORD measured to His people by lot at Shiloh. The dictionary does not press the meaning of the name beyond what Scripture warrants; it honours that the same God who scattereth the chariots of the proud was pleased to give His people a quiet town and call it by that name. When the lot fell, the children of Simeon received their cities within the borders of the children of Judah, for the part of Judah was too much for them (Jos 19:9). He who divided to the nations their inheritance and set the bounds of the people did not overlook this little town of the south (Deu 32:8; Act 17:26). The lines were fallen unto Simeon in pleasant places, and Beth-marcaboth stands as a witness that the strength of nations and the chariots of men are nothing beside the quiet faithfulness of the God who apportions every portion of His people’s heritage.

etymology: Hebrew beyth patstsets, “house of dispersion” or “house of scattering,” a town in the allotment of the tribe of Issachar.
biblical_def: Beth-pazzez was a town reckoned to the tribe of Issachar when Joshua and Eleazar the priest divided the land by lot. It is named near the close of Issachar’s border, set with En-haddah, hard by the coasts of the tribe, among the sixteen cities and their villages that fell to that people (Jos 19:21). The name, the house of scattering, tells us little of its story, for Scripture says no more than that it was there and that it was given; and the dictionary is content to let the silence stand. What it honours is that Issachar, the strong ass couching down between two burdens, received a measured and settled portion in the good land, and that this little town was part of it. He who divided to the nations their inheritance and set the bounds of the people did not pass over Beth-pazzez when the lot came up at Shiloh (Deu 32:8; Act 17:26). The lines were fallen unto Issachar in pleasant places, and not one of the LORD’s good promises failed; all came to pass (Jos 21:45). Beth-pazzez stands as a witness that a name we barely understand was nonetheless a real place in a real inheritance, kept and given by the God who forgets none of His people’s portions.

etymology: Hebrew beyth pelet, “house of escape” or “house of deliverance,” a town of the south country in the allotment of Judah.
biblical_def: Beth-phelet, the house of escape, was a town of the Negeb reckoned to the tribe of Judah in the uttermost south, named among the cities toward the coast of Edom (Jos 15:27). It is a place that endured, for after the captivity the children of Judah dwelt there again, and Beth-phelet is named among the towns repeopled in the days of Nehemiah (Neh 11:26). The name, the house of deliverance, is fitting for a town that outlived the sword and the exile and saw its people return; though Scripture does not draw the lesson, the dictionary may reverently observe how aptly the LORD names the dwellings of His people. He who divided to the nations their inheritance and set the bounds of the people gave Beth-phelet to Judah at the first, and the same faithful God brought a remnant back to it after the chastening of the captivity (Deu 32:8; Act 17:26). The lines were fallen unto Judah in pleasant places, and not one good word of the LORD failed. Beth-phelet stands a witness that the house of escape is no empty name, for the God who apportions the land is the God who preserves and restores His people’s portion through every judgment.

etymology: Hebrew beyth tsur, “house of rock” or “house of the rock,” a town of the hill country of Judah, afterward fortified by Rehoboam.
biblical_def: Beth-zur, the house of rock, was a town set in the hill country of the tribe of Judah, named among the cities of the mountain in the apportioning of the land (Jos 15:58). It stood upon high and rocky ground south of Jerusalem, and its strength of position was not lost upon the kings of Judah, for Rehoboam built it up among the cities of defence in Judah and in Benjamin, fortifying it against the enemies of the south (2Ch 11:7). The name fits the place, a house upon the rock; and the dictionary may reverently mark how the LORD set His people on stony heights of refuge. He who divided to the nations their inheritance and set the bounds of the people gave Beth-zur to Judah at the lot, and afterward it was a stronghold in the day of trouble (Deu 32:8; Act 17:26). The lines were fallen unto Judah in pleasant places, and even the rocky hill was numbered among the goodly heritage. Beth-zur stands as a witness that the strength of a fenced city is from the LORD, and that the saint’s sure defence is not in walls of stone but in the Rock that is higher than himself, the God who apportions and keeps His people’s portion.

etymology: Hebrew beyth biri, “house of my creation” or “house of my Creator,” a dwelling place of the tribe of Simeon recorded in the genealogies of Chronicles.
biblical_def: Beth-birei was a dwelling place of the children of Simeon, named in the record of their cities and villages set down in the first book of the Chronicles. There the chronicler tells how the families of Simeon dwelt at Beersheba and Moladah and the other towns of their portion, “and at Beth-birei, and at Shaaraim. These were their cities unto the reign of David” (1Ch 4:31). It was therefore a settled habitation of Simeon within the wide inheritance of Judah, held until the days of the king, when the line of the towns was written down for a memorial. The name, the house of the Creator, is a fair one for a dwelling of the covenant people; and the dictionary marks how the LORD set His name even upon the small towns of His least tribe. He who divided to the nations their inheritance and set the bounds of the people did not pass over Beth-birei when He apportioned the south to Simeon (Deu 32:8; Act 17:26). The lines were fallen unto Simeon in pleasant places, and Beth-birei stands a witness that the God who made the ends of the earth wrote down by name the very houses where His people dwelt.

etymology: Hebrew beyth meon, “house of habitation” or “house of dwelling,” a city of the high plain of Moab named in the burden pronounced by the prophet Jeremiah.
biblical_def: Beth-meon was a city of the tableland of Moab, named in the long burden the LORD spake against Moab by the prophet Jeremiah. When judgment was declared upon the pride of Moab, the prophet numbered her cities one by one that should fall, and among them is Beth-meon, that the word of the LORD might be sure against every stronghold of her boasting (Jer 48:23). The town had once belonged to the inheritance east of the Jordan, in the country Israel took from Sihon, and was reckoned to Reuben in the apportioning; but it had fallen again under Moab, and so came under the burden of the prophet. The dictionary records it that the reader may see how the LORD knows the names of the cities even of His enemies, and brings down the high places of pride. He who divided to the nations their inheritance and set the bounds of the people likewise appoints the times of their judgment (Deu 32:8; Act 17:26). Beth-meon, the house of dwelling, was made a desolation, that men might learn that no habitation stands sure against the word of God. The same providence that apportions the land also visits it, and the saint takes warning that the LORD is righteous in all His judgments.

etymology: Hebrew beyth eden, “house of pleasure” or “house of delight,” a place of Aram, named “the house of Eden” in the prophet Amos.
biblical_def: Beth-eden, “the house of Eden,” was a seat of power in Aram named in the burden the prophet Amos pronounced against Damascus and the kingdoms of Syria. When the LORD declared He would send a fire into the house of Hazael that should devour the palaces of Ben-hadad, He added that He would break the bar of Damascus and cut off the inhabitant from the plain of Aven, “and him that holdeth the sceptre from the house of Eden” (Amo 1:5). It was therefore a place of rule and pleasure among the Syrians, its very name boasting of delight; yet the word of the LORD was against it, and the sceptre held there should be cut off. The dictionary records it that the reader may see how the LORD humbles the proud seats of the nations, and how a house called by the name of Eden cannot keep its pleasure when God is against it. He who set the bounds of the people also brings down the mighty from their thrones (Deu 32:8; Act 17:26). Beth-eden stands a witness that no garden of man’s making, however named, endures against the judgment of the God who alone gives and keeps the true paradise of His people.

etymology: Hebrew rimmon perets, “pomegranate of the breach” or “Rimmon of the breach,” one of the encampments of Israel in the wilderness wanderings.
biblical_def: Rimmon-perez was one of the stations of the children of Israel in their journeyings through the wilderness, written down by Moses at the commandment of the LORD. As the camp moved from place to place from Rameses unto the plains of Moab, Moses wrote their goings out according to their journeys, and among these is Rimmon-perez, set between Rithmah and Libnah in the long roll of the wandering (Num 33:19-20). It was a bare halting-place in the desert, named perhaps for a pomegranate tree in a broken and rocky ground, where Israel pitched and afterward removed. The dictionary records it because the Spirit of God thought it worth recording, for Moses was commanded to write these journeys, that the generations after might trace the faithfulness of the LORD who led His people every step (Num 33:2). He who divided to the nations their inheritance and set the bounds of the people guided Israel from camp to camp toward the promised land (Deu 32:8; Act 17:26). Rimmon-perez stands a witness that the LORD numbers even the resting-places of His pilgrim people, and that not one stage of the wilderness way is forgotten by the God who brings His own at last into their rest.

etymology: Hebrew rimmon, “pomegranate,” a town of the south country given first to Judah and then reckoned to the tribe of Simeon.
biblical_def: Rimmon was a town of the uttermost south, named among the cities of Judah toward the coast of Edom and afterward reckoned to the tribe of Simeon, whose portion was drawn out of the large inheritance of Judah (Jos 15:32; 19:7). It was a real and abiding place, for it is named again by the prophet Zechariah in the day of the LORD, when he foretells that all the land should be turned as a plain “from Geba to Rimmon south of Jerusalem” (Zec 14:10), marking the southern bound of the land that should be lifted up and inhabited. The name, the pomegranate, fits a town of the fruitful south; and the dictionary honours how the LORD set His people in a land of vines and pomegranates and good things. He who divided to the nations their inheritance and set the bounds of the people gave Rimmon to His people at the lot, and named it again in the latter-day promise (Deu 32:8; Act 17:26). The lines were fallen unto them in pleasant places. Rimmon stands a witness that the God who apportioned the south at the conquest is the same who holds it in His promise to the end, faithful in the first dividing and in the last gathering of His people’s portion.
